progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From B8: mutation is a change in the base sequence and the only way a brand-new allele appears; reshuffling (crossing over, independent assortment, random fertilisation) makes new combinations of existing alleles; a mutation is inherited only if it is in a cell that makes eggs or sperm. From B4 and B5a: DNA copying is accurate, not perfect; most errors are repaired; a surviving error is copied into every descendant cell. From B7: the sickle cell allele is one base change in the haemoglobin gene. From B6a: a bacterium's circular chromosome; plasmids can carry resistance genes. From B6b: a gene codes for a product. Year 11: natural selection, selection pressure. Not assumed: gene pool, population-level allele language, random with respect to need, replica plating, gene flow.
progression.startsWith: The Module 6 opener. The video opens: In 1945, Alexander Fleming, the scientist who discovered penicillin, gave a warning in his Nobel Prize lecture.
progression.stopsAfter: defining gene, allele and gene pool and keeping the three levels apart; saying that a base change inside a gene makes a new allele (sickle cell); saying that a new allele starts as one copy in one individual and that many mutations change nothing visible; explaining how a new allele is passed on in bacteria (both daughter cells) and in animals (only from cells that make eggs or sperm); explaining random with respect to need and the replica plating evidence; explaining how an antibiotic selects an existing resistance allele and raises its frequency; separating mutation (makes alleles), meiosis and fertilisation (mix them), gene flow (moves them, so it can add an allele new to a population) and selection and chance (change frequency); applying this to an unseen evaluate item on rifampicin resistance and an unseen classification of three events in an island lizard population.
progression.nextLesson: how mutagens increase DNA damage (route entry bio-m6-b02), then what one changed base can do to a protein (bio-m6-b03).

teaching.task: How does one changed base in one organism end up as a new allele in a whole population's gene pool, and did the antibiotic cause it?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why a base change makes a new allele (the gene's sequence is now different, 3); why a new allele starts rare (one cell, one individual, 4); why many mutations change nothing visible (outside genes, same protein, 4); why bacteria pass every mutation on (division copies the whole chromosome, 5); why an animal's skin-cell mutation is not inherited (not in an egg or sperm line, 5); why mutation can't be for resistance (a bacterium can't sense the drug and choose a change, 6); how we know (replica plates, 7); why resistance rises (differential survival and division, 8); why gene flow can add an allele without a mutation in that population (9).
teaching.conversationalApproach: Fleming's 1945 warning sets the question (did penicillin make the bacteria change, or were some already different?); three levels (gene, allele, gene pool) are built on screen before they are named; one base change becomes one copy in one individual, then spreads by division in bacteria or through eggs and sperm in animals; the replica plates answer the hook; penicillin is shown selecting, not creating; the processes are sorted into make, mix, move and change frequency. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Fleming warned that too little penicillin could leave resistant survivors, and resistance did spread. So did penicillin make the bacteria change, or were some of them already different before the drug arrived?
teaching.understandingCheck: 12a is an evaluate item on a Staphylococcus aureus infection (10^10 bacteria, 1 in 10^8 rifampicin resistant before treatment, five days of rifampicin alone, most survivors resistant) with the claim "The rifampicin caused the bacteria to mutate so they could survive": it tests random mutation before exposure (about 100 resistant cells already), selection as differential survival and division, and inheritance in bacteria; crossed mistake "bacteria mutate because they need to". 12c classifies three events in an island lizard population (a germ-line base change, a new combination of existing alleles, the same change in a skin cell): yes, no, no; crossed mistake "every mutation enters the gene pool". Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; each card stays on screen during and after the countdown; feedback about 27 to 30 s.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (2017, BIO12-13, programme/syllabus/bio-2017-y12.json, B6-IQ1-02, p 51): "compare the causes, processes and effects of different types of mutation, including but not limited to: point mutation; chromosomal mutation". This video supplies the shared frame for that dotpoint (cause, process, effect on a gene pool) and answers the inquiry question "How does mutation introduce new alleles into a population?"; the comparison of mutation types is b03 and b04, mutagens b02.

design.visualSystem: Three boards, one at a time. (1) The level board (scenes 2 to 4): a slim coded DNA strand (SlimStrand: two thin lines with rungs, a soft gene band, one highlighted position with a before/after base callout), beside a population of small b6a-bacterium-v1.png plates, each with a coded allele ring (open: original allele; amber notched: new allele; never colour alone). (2) The population board (scenes 5 to 8, 10): a dividing Lineage tree copying the ring to both daughters; the replica plating sequence on the m6-agar-dish-top-v1.png and m6-velvet-replica-block-v1.png plates with coded colony dots at fixed positions; a DayStrip for the penicillin course; animals as B8's fly plates, never people. (3) The source board (scene 9, memory, decision rule): four process chips around a coded gene pool basin. Amber marks the new allele only. Reuse: the explainer kit (Plate, Callout, Mark, Countdown, HandText, DrawPath, scribbleEllipse, Enter), B6a's WrongChip, GreyTag, Cross, Cam; m6-red-cells-normal-sickle-v1.png; m6-uv-skin-v1.png for the next chip.
design.transitionPlan: The 1945 card and the bacterium cluster open with the two question chips; the level board builds strand, allele pair and pool basin in turn; the population board takes over as the marked bacterium divides and the fly panel splits off; the hook's chips return for randomness and the replica plates resolve them with a tick and a cross; the population falls away to its resistant lineage under the day strip; the source board gathers make, mix and move around the basin; three frequency lines show what happens next; each attempt clears the board and its feedback shrinks the card to a strip and builds the model answer one point at a time; the step chips and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
